Keywords: Dynamic lighting is a potentially promising solution to meet the individual’s chronobiologic and psychological
Dynamic lighting needs at specific times of day or for specific activities. Yet, few studies have investigated the impact of dynamic
Well-being lighting patterns on daytime functioning and nocturnal sleep, and the optimal dynamic lighting pattern remains
Task performance
largely unknown. The current study assessed the effects of a daylong dynamic lighting (DL) pattern with mod-
Sleep quality
ulations in intensity and spectrum vs. static office lighting (SL) on markers of well-being, cognitive performance,
Office environment
visual experiences, and sleep in a simulated office environment. Twenty-one subjects participated in the 48-h
balanced crossover laboratory study. The findings revealed time-of-day and experimental-day dependent bene-
fits of the DL vs. SL pattern on daytime vitality, sleepiness, state self-control, mood, performance on a sustained
attention task and subsequent subjective sleep quality. Complementing earlier research outcomes reported in the
literature, the current study suggests that a dynamic lighting approach could be a practical strategy to support
office workers’ daytime well-being and nocturnal sleep. Yet, the results revealed no consistent pattern across
assessments nor across the different types of metrics at a specific assessment, thus additional research regarding
the optimization of lighting parameters and pattern is needed.

No statistically significant benefits of the employed dynamic vs. static
lighting were revealed in terms of task performance, visual experiences
during the day and sleep quality during the night. To date, what dy-
namic lighting pattern is optimal to benefit daytime psychological
functioning and night-time sleep still remains largely unknown. In the
current laboratory study, a new dynamic lighting scenario was created
and the impact of this dynamic profile on daytime alertness, mood and
performance, visual experiences and night-time sleep was investigated.
This focus on multiple aspects related to health and performance aligns
with the recently introduced concept of integrative lighting, i.e., indoor
healthy lighting which integrates the occupant’s visual requirements as
well as chronobiologic and psychological needs, by CIE [11].
